courses.title: Environmental and Occupational Health
courses.description: Water supply and sanitation, waste management, air pollution, housing and vector control, food safety, and occupational health and safety in Nigeria.

topics.title: Water Supply and Water-related Diseases
topics.summary: Sources, quality standards, treatment of water and classification of water-related diseases.

material.heading: Water and disease
material.body: Safe water is essential for health. Sources: surface water (rivers, streams, ponds — often contaminated), groundwater (wells, boreholes — generally safer if protected) and rainwater. The WHO standard for drinking water is zero E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) per 100 mL — faecal indicator bacteria. Bradley's classification of water-related diseases: water-borne (ingested — cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A and E, dysentery), water-washed (due to lack of water for hygiene — scabies, trachoma, diarrhoea), water-based (a part of the life cycle in an aquatic host — schistosomiasis, guinea worm/dracunculiasis, now nearly eradicated) and water-related insect vector diseases (malaria, onchocerciasis, trypanosomiasis).
keyPoints: Drinking water: 0 E. coli per 100 mL

material.heading: Water treatment
material.body: Large-scale treatment: storage and sedimentation, coagulation/flocculation (alum), rapid or slow sand filtration (slow sand filters have a biological 'schmutzdecke' layer), and disinfection by chlorination — the most widely used method; the target residual free chlorine at the tap is about 0.2–0.5 mg/L. Household water treatment: boiling (rolling boil for 1 minute), chlorination (e.g. sodium hypochlorite drops such as WaterGuard), solar disinfection (SODIS — clear plastic bottles in sunlight for 6 hours), ceramic or biosand filters, and safe storage in covered containers with a tap. Chlorine demand must be satisfied before a free residual exists (breakpoint chlorination).

topics.title: Sanitation and Waste Management
topics.summary: Excreta disposal, latrines, solid waste and health-care waste management.

material.heading: Excreta disposal
material.body: Safe disposal of human excreta breaks faecal–oral transmission ('F-diagram': fluids, fields, flies, fingers and food). Improved sanitation facilities include flush/pour-flush toilets to sewers or septic tanks, ventilated improved pit (VIP) latrines (a vent pipe with fly screen reduces odour and flies), pit latrines with slabs and composting toilets. Latrines should be at least 30 metres from a water source and above the water table. Nigeria has one of the largest populations practising open defecation; the 'Clean Nigeria: Use the Toilet' campaign and community-led total sanitation (CLTS) aim to end it.
keyPoints: F-diagram: fluids, fields, flies, fingers, food
VIP latrine: vent pipe with fly screen

material.heading: Solid and health-care waste
material.body: Solid waste management involves storage, collection, transport, treatment and disposal: sanitary landfill (compacted and covered daily — preferred), composting, incineration and recycling (reduce, reuse, recycle). Open dumping and burning cause vector breeding, flooding (blocked drains) and air pollution. Health-care waste: about 75–90% is general non-hazardous waste; the rest is hazardous (infectious, sharps, pathological, pharmaceutical, chemical, radioactive). Segregate at the point of generation using colour-coded bins (commonly yellow for infectious, black for general, red or labelled boxes for anatomical waste, puncture-proof safety boxes for sharps), store safely and treat by autoclaving, incineration or other approved methods.
keyPoints: Segregate at source with colour codes

topics.title: Air Pollution, Housing and Vector Control
topics.summary: Indoor and outdoor air pollution, healthy housing, and control of mosquitoes, flies and rodents.

material.heading: Air pollution and housing
material.body: Household air pollution from cooking with firewood, charcoal and kerosene in poorly ventilated kitchens is a major cause of pneumonia in children, COPD in women, low birth weight and cataracts; cleaner fuels (LPG, electricity), improved cookstoves and ventilation reduce exposure. Outdoor pollutants: particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10 — penetrate deep into the lungs), nitrogen and sulphur oxides, ozone and carbon monoxide from vehicles, generators, industry, gas flaring (Niger Delta) and the dry-season Harmattan dust. Carbon monoxide poisoning from generators used indoors is a recurrent cause of deaths in Nigeria. Healthy housing requires adequate space (avoid overcrowding — spreads TB and meningitis), ventilation, lighting, safe water, sanitation, drainage and protection from vectors.

material.heading: Vector control
material.body: Malaria vector (Anopheles) control: long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs), indoor residual spraying (IRS), larval source management (draining stagnant water, larviciding), and window screens. Aedes mosquitoes (yellow fever, dengue) breed in containers such as tyres, pots and cans — remove them. Integrated vector management combines methods and monitors insecticide resistance. Houseflies transmit diarrhoeal diseases and trachoma — control through sanitation and waste management. Rodent control (proofing, food storage, traps, environmental cleanliness) prevents Lassa fever and leptospirosis; store food in rodent-proof containers and do not dry food on open ground.

topics.title: Food Hygiene and Safety
topics.summary: Food-borne diseases, food handlers, WHO five keys to safer food, and food regulation.

material.heading: Food-borne disease
material.body: Food-borne diseases result from biological (Salmonella, E. coli, Campylobacter, Vibrio cholerae, Staphylococcus aureus toxin, Bacillus cereus, Clostridium perfringens, hepatitis A, parasites), chemical (pesticide residues, aflatoxins from mouldy grains and groundnuts — liver cancer; calcium carbide ripening of fruits; formalin on fish; bromate in bread) and physical hazards. WHO 'Five Keys to Safer Food': keep clean; separate raw and cooked food; cook thoroughly (core temperature ≥ 70 °C); keep food at safe temperatures (the danger zone is 5–60 °C; refrigerate below 5 °C; do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours); use safe water and raw materials.
keyPoints: Aflatoxins in mouldy grains → liver cancer
WHO Five Keys to Safer Food

material.heading: Food handlers and regulation
material.body: Food handlers need medical screening (e.g. for typhoid carriage, TB, skin infections), training in personal hygiene, handwashing, protective clothing and exclusion when ill with diarrhoea, vomiting or infected wounds. Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) is a systematic preventive approach used in food industries. In Nigeria, NAFDAC regulates processed foods, the Standards Organisation of Nigeria sets standards, and environmental health officers inspect food premises, markets and abattoirs (meat inspection prevents zoonoses such as tuberculosis and taeniasis).

topics.title: Occupational Health and Safety
topics.summary: Occupational hazards, occupational diseases, pre-employment and periodic examinations, and legislation.

material.heading: Hazards and diseases
material.body: Occupational hazards are physical (noise — noise-induced hearing loss above ~85 dB(A); heat; vibration; radiation), chemical (dusts — silicosis, asbestosis, coal workers' pneumoconiosis, byssinosis in cotton workers; solvents; lead — anaemia, neuropathy; pesticides — organophosphate poisoning), biological (TB, hepatitis B, anthrax in hide handlers, leptospirosis), ergonomic (musculoskeletal disorders, back pain) and psychosocial (stress, shift work, violence). Artisanal gold mining with lead-contaminated ore caused a major lead poisoning outbreak in Zamfara State (2010) that killed hundreds of children.

material.heading: Prevention and law
material.body: Occupational health services provide pre-placement (pre-employment) medical examination, periodic examinations and biological monitoring (e.g. blood lead, cholinesterase for pesticide workers), health education, workplace surveillance, first aid and emergency care, immunisation (hepatitis B for health workers), and rehabilitation. Controls follow the hierarchy: elimination, substitution, engineering controls (ventilation, guarding machines), administrative controls (job rotation, training, reduced exposure time) and personal protective equipment (last resort). Nigerian legislation includes the Factories Act (1990) and the Employee's Compensation Act (2010), administered with the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund (NSITF), which compensates workers for occupational injuries and diseases.

questions.stem: Noise-induced hearing loss becomes a risk with prolonged exposure above about:
